text:
The ozone hole forms because Antarctic winter creates extremely cold stratospheric conditions, producing polar stratospheric clouds. Their surfaces convert stable chlorine reservoirs (like HCl and ClONO₂) into reactive forms such as Cl₂ and HOCl. The polar vortex, a strong circulation that isolates the air, keeps these reactions concentrated.

Spring brings sunlight back. When sunlight returns, it splits Cl₂ and other compounds, releasing chlorine radicals that catalytically destroy ozone (O₃) at enormous rates. Ozone loss peaks in September and October, then the hole gradually closes as the vortex breaks down and fresh ozone-rich air mixes in.
